issues.title: Missed optimization with match on repr(i8) enum
issues.body:
The following functions *ought* to be equivalent:

```rust
use core::cmp::Ordering;

pub fn test1(call: fn() -> Ordering) -> i32 {
    match call() {
        Ordering::Less => -1,
        Ordering::Equal => 0,
        Ordering::Greater => 1,
    }
}

pub fn test2(call: fn() -> Ordering) -> i32 {
    call() as i32
}
```
but compile to the following x86_64 assembly on play.rust-lang.org:
```assembly
playground::test1:
	pushq	%rax
	callq	*%rdi
	incb	%al
	movzbl	%al, %eax
	decl	%eax
	popq	%rcx
	retq

playground::test2:
	pushq	%rax
	callq	*%rdi
	movsbl	%al, %eax
	popq	%rcx
	retq
```

for both stable (1.66.0) and nightly (1.68.0-nightly 2023-01-03 c7572670a1302f5c7e24).

analysis.summary: The PR extends MatchBranchSimplification with a new SimplifyToExp strategy: when a SwitchInt over an enum discriminant has between 2 and 64 distinct targets, all targets share the same terminator, the otherwise target is empty-unreachable, and every arm assigns the value equal to its discriminant value (possibly after an integer cast), the switch/arm chain can be replaced by a single `_0 = <discriminant> as RetTy (IntToInt)` assignment. The reusable correctness core is the negative side of that pattern: the rewrite is only valid when each arm constant actually equals the discriminant value that selects it and when there is no reachable fallback; otherwise the pass must leave the switch intact. The PR adds `_failed` and `_fallback` tests specifically to pin those non-optimizable cases.
analysis.trigger: A basic block ends in `TerminatorKind::SwitchInt` whose discriminant is `Operand::Copy`/`Operand::Move`, with 2..=64 distinct switch targets, an empty-unreachable `otherwise` block, identical terminators in every target, equal statement counts, and each non-identical statement being a constant assignment to the same place whose integer value matches the discriminant value selecting that arm. The discriminant type and the arm constant type may differ (e.g. repr(i8) enum discriminant matched to i16 constants), in which case the pass emits an `IntToInt` cast.
preconditions: All switch targets including the fallback are distinct (`targets.is_distinct()`)
The otherwise target is empty unreachable (`bbs[targets.otherwise()].is_empty_unreachable()`)
All explicit target blocks have the same terminator kind
The first two target blocks have equal statement counts and their statement sequences align one-to-one
For every aligned pair, statements are either identical or integral constant assignments to the same place
Each arm's constant value is checked against the discriminator value selecting that arm; non-matching constants make can_simplify return None
The transformation only fires when mir_opt_level() >= 1
pitfalls: Do not rewrite an arm whose assigned constant differs from its discriminant value: `match_u8_i16_failed` is an EnumAu8 with B=2 but `EnumAu8::B => 3`, and the expected MIR still contains `switchInt`; a naive `ret = discr as T` rewrite would return 2 for B instead of 3.

Do not drop a reachable fallback: `match_u8_i16_fallback` matches a plain u8 with `_ => 3` and its `otherwise` is not unreachable, so the pass must keep the `switchInt`; a rewrite assuming exhaustiveness would return 0 for input 0 instead of 3.

Negative discriminants require signed-aware comparison: patch 4 adds `int_equal` plus `is_signed` to CompareType::Discr, because discriminant values such as 65535 for -1_i16 are not equal to the constant under plain unsigned `ScalarInt::try_from_uint` comparison.

Signedness mismatch between discriminant type and arm-constant type matters: `int_equal` sign-extends at the discriminant size (`l.try_to_int(l.size())` and `ScalarInt::try_from_uint(r, size).try_to_int(size)`), while the emitted rewrite uses `Rvalue::Cast(CastKind::IntToInt, ...)` whose extension follows the source/destination types. A transform must verify that the cast result actually equals the arm constant.

Do not confuse identical-looking statements with value-carrying assignments: the pass only substitutes `Rvalue::Use(discr_local)` or `Rvalue::Cast(CastKind::IntToInt, ...)` for `TransfromType::Discr`; `Same`/`Eq` statements are copied unchanged.
The test comment typo `// CHECH: return` is inert; do not treat a retained old comment or test name as proof of the transformation's output. Compare the actual assignment lines in the expected MIR.

The transformation introduces a temporary, emits StorageLive/move/StorageDead around the cast, and patches the terminator via MirPatch; preserving def-use/storage scoping is required for MIR validity.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation is to collapse the switch purely on the syntactic pattern (all arms assign constants to the same place / same terminator), emitting `_0 = discriminant as RetTy (IntToInt)` without verifying that each arm's constant actually equals the discriminant value that reaches it, and/or without requiring the otherwise block to be unreachable. Concretely: (a) rewriting `match i { EnumAu8::A => 1, EnumAu8::B => 3 }` where `EnumAu8::B` has discriminant 2 into a cast would return 2 instead of 3; (b) rewriting `match i { 1 => 1, 2 => 2, _ => 3 }` into a cast would drop the reachable default and return 0 for input 0 instead of 3. The merged pass prevents both by returning None unless `is_distinct()`, `otherwise().is_empty_unreachable()`, and per-arm constant-vs-discriminant equality (including signed negative cases) all hold. A second incorrect variant is the pre-patch-4 implementation that compared discriminator values with unsigned `ScalarInt::try_from_uint` only: it silently failed to optimize negative/signed cases rather than emitting the cast.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust functions matching over a `#[repr(u8)]`, `#[repr(i8)]`, `#[repr(i16)]`, or `#[repr(i128)]` enum (or a plain integer) where every match arm returns an integral constant. Differential pairs: a transformable case such as `#[repr(u8)] enum E { A=1, B=2 } fn f(e: E) -> i16 { match e { E::A => 1, E::B => 2 } }` (safe to replace with `e as i16`), versus `fn f(e: E) -> i16 { match e { E::A => 1, E::B => 3 } }` (constant 3 != discriminant 2, must stay a switch), versus `fn f(i: u8) -> i16 { match i { 1 => 1, 2 => 2, _ => 3 } }` (reachable fallback, must stay a switch). Also include negative discriminant cases like `#[repr(i16)] enum E { A=-1, B=2, C=-3 }` and wide cases like `#[repr(i128)]` with `u128::MAX`. Custom-MIR blocks are used to vary instruction lengths/statement counts.
analysis.testStrategy: Pair programs that differ only in whether the arm constants match the discriminants, and observe the MatchBranchSimplification MIR dump. Positive cases should assert `// CHECK-NOT: switchInt` and `// CHECK: _0 = _3 as i16 (IntToInt);` (e.g. match_u8_i16, match_u8_u16, match_i8_i16, match_i16_i8, match_i128_u128). Negative cases should assert `// CHECK: switchInt` (match_u8_i16_failed, match_i8_i16_failed, match_u8_i16_fallback). Add `_2` custom-MIR variants with different instruction lengths/duplicate assignments and assert the switch is preserved when the pattern does not align. Run the pass with `//@ unit-test: MatchBranchSimplification` and `// EMIT_MIR <fn>.MatchBranchSimplification.diff`; do not infer pass behavior from test names or old comments alone.
analysis.originalLogic: Before the new SimplifyToExp branch, MatchBranchSimplification only simplified a SwitchInt with exactly one explicit value whose two targets were identical except for bool constant assignments (SimplifyToIf, producing `_0 = Eq/Ne(discr, val)`). An exhaustive enum match on a repr(u8/i8/...) enum whose arms simply return the discriminant value remained a `switchInt` chain with one constant assignment per arm, even though the values were equivalent to a single integer cast.
